title: Does College Pedigree Predict NBA Career Length?
text: “Blue blood” college basketball programs — Duke, North Carolina, UCLA, Indiana, Kentucky, and Kansas — are historically dominant and heavily recruited from. The question: does attending one of these programs actually predict a longer NBA career, or is that reputation not backed up by the data? This matters to a recruit choosing a school and to a front office comparing two draft prospects.

title: Does College Pedigree Predict NBA Career Length?
text: “Blue blood” college basketball programs — Duke, North Carolina, UCLA, Indiana, Kentucky, and Kansas — are historically dominant and heavily recruited from. The question: does attending one of these programs actually predict a longer NBA career, or is that reputation not backed up by the data? This matters to a recruit choosing a school and to a front office comparing two draft prospects.

title: Does College Pedigree Predict NBA Career Length?
text:
Data & Method
Using publicly available NBA player records (Kaggle), we computed each player’s total years played and split the sample into blue-blood alumni and everyone else. Career length is a non-negative, discrete, right-skewed variable (most careers are short; a few are very long), which makes a Poisson-Gamma conjugate model a natural fit — the Poisson likelihood models the count of years played, and the Gamma prior (informed via data augmentation, with different shape parameters for each group reflecting our prior expectation of ~5 years for blue-blood alumni vs. ~3.5 for others) yields a closed-form posterior.
We were explicit about the model’s main limitation: years played within a single career aren’t truly independent (a player who’s already played 5 seasons is far more likely to play a 6th than a rookie is to play a 2nd), which the model can’t capture. We treated this as a known simplification rather than pretending the assumption held.

title: Does College Pedigree Predict NBA Career Length?
text:
Results

95% credible interval for mean career length: (5.09, 5.51) years for blue-blood alumni vs. (4.27, 4.40) years for everyone else
95% credible interval for the difference in means: (0.74, 1.19) years — meaning there’s a 95% posterior probability the true gap falls in that range
Posterior predictive probability of a career longer than 5 years: 42.8% for blue-blood alumni vs. 27.1% for others
Posterior predictive probability of a career longer than 10 years: 1.8% vs. 0.76%

The data support a real gap: blue-blood alumni have measurably longer expected NBA careers.

title: Does College Pedigree Predict NBA Career Length?
text:
Limitations
Career length is only one definition of “success” — it says nothing about points per game, awards, or team accomplishments. The “blue blood” label is also static; some programs on that list (UCLA, for instance) have struggled in recent years and arguably shouldn’t be grouped with currently-dominant programs. A follow-up analysis could control for draft position, era, and position, or use a more current definition of blue-blood status.
Skills demonstrated: Bayesian conjugate modeling (Poisson-Gamma), credible interval interpretation, posterior predictive probability, explicit reasoning about violated modeling assumptions.
Final project for Introduction to Bayesian Statistics (BYU Statistics, STAT 251), with Jonas Schiel.

title: The Great Sleepover(option 1)
text:
A striker is 9-for-10 on penalties

It’s a shootout Saturday. Is he your designated taker?

Raw math says 90%. Your gut says “…it’s ten kicks.”


Ten kicks is a grainy photo. You can’t tell a face from a smudge.


What helps is what you already know about what you’re looking at: penalties go in about three in four times. That’s a prior.

Setup only. The tension: the raw number is the only thing on screen, but you carry two pieces of information, the league rate and his ten kicks. Bayesian statistics is the rule for combining them.

title: The Great Sleepover(option 1)
text:
Prior + evidence = posterior

\[
\theta \sim \text{Beta}(31,\,9) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\theta \mid \text{9 makes, 1 miss} \sim \text{Beta}(40,\,10)
\]


The update is addition: 31 + 9 makes, 9 + 1 miss. And the answer is a distribution, so you can ask: how likely is he actually better than average?

Prior Beta(31, 9), mean 77.5%, worth about 40 kicks. Posterior Beta(40, 10), mean 80%. A decision-maker doesn’t need “80%.” They need “two in three odds he’s better than average, and here’s how much to trust that.” A point estimate can’t give you that.

title: The Great Sleepover(option 1)
section: The prior is an assumption, said out loud
text:
The prior is an assumption, said out loud



With ten kicks, your assumption matters. With a hundred, the data takes over. More exposures sharpen the picture.


Every model has a prior. A model that doesn’t show you one is still using it.

Weak prior is worth about 4 kicks, moderate about 40, strong about 100. The usual objection to Bayes is “isn’t the prior just your opinion?” Answer: yes, and it is stated, adjustable, and overwhelmed by evidence. This sets up the NBA project: thousands of players is the right-hand panel.

title: The Great Sleepover(option 1)
section: My own project: does pedigree predict a longer NBA career?
text:
My own project: does pedigree predict a longer NBA career?

With Jonas Schiel. “Blue blood” programs: Duke, North Carolina, UCLA, Indiana, Kentucky, Kansas.

Career length is a count, right-skewed. Model: Poisson likelihood, Gamma prior. Prior expectation: about 5 years for blue-blood alumni, about 3.5 for everyone else.


Same logic as the penalties. Different conjugate pair, much more data.










Numbers from your write-up: 95% CI for mean career length (5.09, 5.51) vs (4.27, 4.40); difference (0.74, 1.19). Likely questions: (1) “Didn’t you pick different priors for each group?” Yes (5 vs 3.5 years). With this much data the intervals are driven by the data, but the cleanest answer is a sensitivity check: refit with the SAME prior for both groups and report that the conclusion holds. Do this before you present if you can; it turns a vulnerability into the strongest slide. (2) “Is Poisson right?” Poisson forces variance = mean and allows zero years; real careers are overdispersed and at least one year. Say you treated it as a known simplification (your write-up already does) and that a negative binomial or zero-truncated model would be the next step.

What predicts an NHL player’s plus-minus?

With Claire Peterson and Anzlei Larsen. Multiple linear regression, 1,000-iteration cross-validation, NHL seasons 2000-01 to 2024-25.

title: Forecasting Company Growth: Comparing Four Modeling Approaches
text:
Working as if consulting for a discretionary-spending company (products that sell well in strong economies and slow down in downturns), the task was to forecast quarterly percentage growth using macroeconomic indicators — income, industrial production, savings rate, and unemployment — spanning 1975 to 2024.
The real question wasn’t just “can we forecast growth,” but which forecasting approach actually generalizes to unseen future quarters, since a model that fits historical data well can still fail badly out of sample if it’s overfit to noise or ignores the time structure entirely.

title: Forecasting Company Growth: Comparing Four Modeling Approaches
text:
Working as if consulting for a discretionary-spending company (products that sell well in strong economies and slow down in downturns), the task was to forecast quarterly percentage growth using macroeconomic indicators — income, industrial production, savings rate, and unemployment — spanning 1975 to 2024.
The real question wasn’t just “can we forecast growth,” but which forecasting approach actually generalizes to unseen future quarters, since a model that fits historical data well can still fail badly out of sample if it’s overfit to noise or ignores the time structure entirely.

title: Forecasting Company Growth: Comparing Four Modeling Approaches
text:
Approach
Rather than settling on one method, I built and compared four forecasting approaches on the same train/test split (trained on data before 2010–2019 depending on the model, validated on the years after):

Baseline linear regression on the macroeconomic predictors alone, ignoring time structure
ARIMA with exogenous regressors, letting the model capture autocorrelation in growth that the macro variables alone miss
Prophet, a component-based forecasting model, extended with the same macroeconomic regressors
A regression with a natural spline on time plus a quarterly seasonal term, to flexibly capture trend and seasonality without assuming a rigid time-series structure

Each model was evaluated by out-of-sample RMSE on the held-out years — not by how well it fit the training data.

title: Forecasting Company Growth: Comparing Four Modeling Approaches
text:
Results
The plain linear regression, trained only on pre-2010 data, achieved an out-of-sample RMSE of about 0.42 percentage points on post-2010 quarterly growth — a reasonable baseline, but one that ignores any autocorrelation or seasonal pattern in the data. Adding explicit time structure (through ARIMA’s autoregressive terms or the spline-plus-season regression) let the later models capture patterns the baseline missed, illustrating a common trade-off in forecasting: a simple model is easy to explain, but a model that respects the time-series structure of the data usually forecasts better.

title: Forecasting Company Growth: Comparing Four Modeling Approaches
text:
Why This Matters
This mirrors a very common real-world analyst task: given a business metric and some plausible drivers, build not just a model but the right kind of model, and be able to defend that choice against genuine competitors rather than assuming the first approach was correct. That skill — comparing multiple legitimate modeling frameworks head-to-head on held-out data — applies directly to demand forecasting, revenue projection, and economic scenario planning in industry.
Skills demonstrated: time series forecasting (ARIMA, Prophet), regression with splines and seasonality, rigorous out-of-sample model comparison, R (forecast, prophet, splines).
Mini-project for Analysis of Correlated Data (BYU Statistics), with Emily Dunham and Timothy Hardy.

title: Do Early-Season Wildfires Predict a Worse Fire Year?
text: Wildfires are usually analyzed event-by-event — one fire, one size, one cause. This project (with a co-author) instead treats an entire year’s worth of fire activity as a single curve, and asks a shape-of-the-year question: does the monthly pattern of fire counts early in the year predict how much area burns later that year — and does using only past months (rather than the whole year) actually help or hurt prediction?

title: Do Early-Season Wildfires Predict a Worse Fire Year?
text: Wildfires are usually analyzed event-by-event — one fire, one size, one cause. This project (with a co-author) instead treats an entire year’s worth of fire activity as a single curve, and asks a shape-of-the-year question: does the monthly pattern of fire counts early in the year predict how much area burns later that year — and does using only past months (rather than the whole year) actually help or hurt prediction?

title: Do Early-Season Wildfires Predict a Worse Fire Year?
text:
The Data
We used the USDA/US Forest Service wildfire occurrence dataset, which logs individual wildfires reported across the United States from 1992–2020, including discovery date, containment date, fire size, and location. We aggregated these into monthly national summaries, producing two functional (curve-valued) observations per year: a monthly fire-count curve and a monthly mean-area-burned curve.

title: Do Early-Season Wildfires Predict a Worse Fire Year?
text:
Method
This is a function-on-function regression problem: predicting one curve from another, not a single number from a single number. We applied the historical functional linear model (Malfait & Ramsay, 2003), which restricts the model so that area burned in month t can only depend on fire counts from months before t — never the future predicting the past, which wouldn’t make scientific sense.
\[Y_i(t) = \alpha(t) + \int_{s<t} \beta(s,t)\, X_i(s)\, ds + \varepsilon_i(t)\]
We compared this against an unrestricted function-on-function model (which allows any month to inform any other month) as a baseline, fitting both with the pffr framework in R’s refund package, using penalized bivariate splines for the coefficient surface and cross-validated smoothing.
# Historical model — the scientifically appropriate constraint
FullModel_Hist <- pffr(
  Y_log ~ ff(X_log, xind = s, limits = 's<t'),
  yind = t, method = "NCV"
)
Both models were trained on 1992–2015 and evaluated on held-out 2016–2020 data using RMSE on the original (non-log) scale.

title: Do Early-Season Wildfires Predict a Worse Fire Year?
text:
Results
The historical model achieved an R² of 0.60, actually outperforming the unrestricted baseline model (R² of 0.568) — despite using strictly less information (no future months). That’s a meaningful finding: enforcing the scientifically correct causal ordering didn’t just make the model more defensible, it made it more accurate, suggesting the extra “future” information in the unrestricted model was mostly noise rather than signal.

title: Do Early-Season Wildfires Predict a Worse Fire Year?
text:
What This Demonstrates

Working with functional/curve-valued data rather than flat tabular data — a less common but increasingly relevant skill for time-series-heavy or sensor-heavy roles
Applying a real, citation-worthy statistical method (not just an off-the-shelf regression) and knowing when the extra complexity is justified
Proper train/test evaluation with a temporal split, appropriate for time-ordered data
Working with a large, messy federal dataset (fire records spanning three decades)

Final project for Functional Data Analysis (BYU Statistics), with Emily Dunham.

title: Does a Risky Procedure Actually Increase Mortality?
text:
Right Heart Catheterization (RHC) is a diagnostic procedure used on critically ill ICU patients. In the raw data, patients who receive RHC die at noticeably higher rates than those who don’t — which raises an uncomfortable question: does the procedure itself increase the risk of death, or are doctors simply choosing to perform it on the patients who were already the sickest?
This is a textbook case of confounding by indication, and it’s a good showcase for why “the numbers say X” is often the wrong takeaway until you’ve asked why the data looks that way.

title: Does a Risky Procedure Actually Increase Mortality?
text:
Right Heart Catheterization (RHC) is a diagnostic procedure used on critically ill ICU patients. In the raw data, patients who receive RHC die at noticeably higher rates than those who don’t — which raises an uncomfortable question: does the procedure itself increase the risk of death, or are doctors simply choosing to perform it on the patients who were already the sickest?
This is a textbook case of confounding by indication, and it’s a good showcase for why “the numbers say X” is often the wrong takeaway until you’ve asked why the data looks that way.

title: Does a Risky Procedure Actually Increase Mortality?
text:
The Data
The dataset comes from a well-known ICU study and includes treatment status (RHC vs. not), survival outcome, and a wide set of pre-treatment confounders — age, income, insurance type, and physiological severity markers like mean blood pressure, heart rate, and organ dysfunction scores. It’s a genuinely messy, high-dimensional dataset, which is part of what makes it a useful exercise: real clinical data rarely comes clean.

title: Does a Risky Procedure Actually Increase Mortality?
text:
Method
I estimated the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT) using propensity score matching:

Fit a logistic regression propensity score model using only pre-treatment variables
Matched 1:1 nearest-neighbor without replacement, using a caliper of 0.2 on the logit propensity score to exclude implausible matches
Checked covariate balance before and after matching with a Love plot and standardized mean differences
Estimated the ATT with a weighted logistic regression on the matched sample, incorporating matching weights

m_out <- matchit(
  formula = ps_formula,
  data = RHC_use,
  method   = "nearest",
  distance = "glm",
  estimand = "ATT",
  ratio    = 1,
  caliper  = 0.2,
  replace  = FALSE
)

fit_att <- glm(survival ~ RHC, data = match.data(m_out),
                family = binomial, weights = weights)
I chose a logistic propensity score for interpretability, a tight-ish caliper to prioritize match quality over sample size, and no replacement to avoid a small number of controls dominating the estimate — a defensible but not the only reasonable set of choices, which is part of the point of the exercise.

title: Does a Risky Procedure Actually Increase Mortality?
text:
Results
Before matching, several key severity measures (APACHE score, mean arterial pressure, organ dysfunction markers) showed large imbalances between treated and control patients. After matching, nearly all covariates fell within a standardized mean difference of ±0.1.
The matched-sample estimate: RHC is associated with an approximately 5.1 percentage point decrease in probability of death (95% CI: −8.1 to −2.1 points, p = 0.001).
That’s the opposite direction of the naive, unadjusted comparison — which is the whole story here. Once you account for the fact that RHC was preferentially given to sicker patients, the picture flips substantially. The matching procedure retained about 86% of treated patients (1,870 of 2,184); the remaining 14% were too clinically extreme to find a comparable control, so the estimate applies to the broader population of treated patients but not to that highest-risk subgroup.

title: Does a Risky Procedure Actually Increase Mortality?
text:
What This Demonstrates

Recognizing and correcting for confounding by indication, not just fitting a model on raw data
Making and defending non-arbitrary modeling choices (caliper, matching ratio, replacement) and understanding their trade-offs
Being explicit about the limits of a causal estimate — who it generalizes to and who it doesn’t
Comfort with a messy, real-world clinical dataset, not a cleaned-up textbook example

Course project for Applied Biostatistics (BYU Statistics). Full analysis code available on request.

title: Mapping NYC Rodent Complaints: A Case Competition Win
text:
New York City’s 311 system logs resident complaints about rodent activity, and the city uses these reports to help direct inspection and control resources. But 311 data has a well-known blind spot: a complaint reflects not just actual rodent activity, but also who is aware of the reporting system, who trusts it, and who has easy access to it. Our team’s challenge for this case competition was to model which factors actually predict confirmed rodent activity by city council district, while being explicit about where the reporting data itself might mislead.
This project won BYU’s 2026 Statistics Case Study Competition.

title: Mapping NYC Rodent Complaints: A Case Competition Win
text:
New York City’s 311 system logs resident complaints about rodent activity, and the city uses these reports to help direct inspection and control resources. But 311 data has a well-known blind spot: a complaint reflects not just actual rodent activity, but also who is aware of the reporting system, who trusts it, and who has easy access to it. Our team’s challenge for this case competition was to model which factors actually predict confirmed rodent activity by city council district, while being explicit about where the reporting data itself might mislead.
This project won BYU’s 2026 Statistics Case Study Competition.

title: Mapping NYC Rodent Complaints: A Case Competition Win
text:
Approach
We classified “confirmed” cases from 311 call descriptions — instances where an inspector found violations or issues were actively being remediated — as distinct from raw complaint volume, since raw call counts conflate actual infestation with reporting behavior. We supplemented 311 data with land use reports and restaurant inspection records as additional predictors.
Because rodent activity naturally clusters geographically (an infested block affects its neighbors), we modeled the confirmed complaint rate using a conditional autoregressive (CAR) model across city council districts, which accounts for spatial correlation rather than treating each district as independent.

title: Mapping NYC Rodent Complaints: A Case Competition Win
text:
Results
The model identified factors associated with an increase in confirmed rodent activity — proximity to other rodent-related issues, higher median home value, and older building stock — alongside factors associated with a decrease, including more people per housing unit and a higher share of vacant units. Confirmed rodent activity also showed a clear seasonal pattern, spiking in summer months.
We translated the model into three concrete recommendations: focus inspection resources on districts with high confirmed (not just reported) rates, shift staffing to anticipate the summer spike, and increase community outreach in underrepresented districts where low reporting likely masks real activity — flagging explicitly that 311 complaint volume alone is not a reliable proxy for actual infestation.

title: Mapping NYC Rodent Complaints: A Case Competition Win
text:
Why This Matters
This project is really about a broader problem: administrative data (311 calls, customer complaints, support tickets) always reflects reporting behavior as much as the underlying phenomenon, and a naive model that ignores that will misallocate resources. Separating “what’s reported” from “what’s real,” and building a spatial model that respects geographic structure, is directly transferable to resource allocation problems in public health, city services, and operations.
Skills demonstrated: spatial statistics (CAR models), working with noisy administrative/reporting data, translating a technical model into policy recommendations, team-based analysis under competition time constraints.

title: Mapping Heat-Related Illness Risk in Houston
text: Heat-related illness isn’t evenly distributed across a city — it concentrates where air conditioning is scarce, where the population skews older or younger, and where poverty limits access to cooling. Working as if contracted by the Houston Health Department, I analyzed census-tract-level heat-illness counts to find out which neighborhood characteristics predict elevated risk, and where the city should focus outreach and resources.

title: Mapping Heat-Related Illness Risk in Houston
text: Heat-related illness isn’t evenly distributed across a city — it concentrates where air conditioning is scarce, where the population skews older or younger, and where poverty limits access to cooling. Working as if contracted by the Houston Health Department, I analyzed census-tract-level heat-illness counts to find out which neighborhood characteristics predict elevated risk, and where the city should focus outreach and resources.

title: Mapping Heat-Related Illness Risk in Houston
text:
The Data
Census-tract-level data covering heat-related illness counts and population, alongside demographic and socioeconomic covariates: median age, percentage Hispanic and Black population, percentage under 5 and over 65, poverty rate, percentage living alone, and minimum temperature.

title: Mapping Heat-Related Illness Risk in Houston
text:
Method
Because neighboring census tracts tend to share similar risk (a hot, low-income area is usually next to another hot, low-income area), treating tracts as independent observations would understate uncertainty and miss spatial structure. I modeled the log relative risk of heat illness using a conditional autoregressive (CAR) model — a spatial regression that explicitly accounts for correlation between neighboring geographic units — fit with the spmodel package in R.
spautor_model <- spautor(
  log_rel_risk ~ MED_AGE + HispanicPC + BlackPCT +
    under5PCT + over65PCT + povertyPCT + alonePCT + MinTemp,
  data = dat_clean, spcov_type = "car"
)
I checked model assumptions with added-variable plots (linearity), residual histograms (normality), and residual-vs-fitted plots (equal variance) before finalizing the model, and reported pseudo-R² as a goodness-of-fit measure.

title: Mapping Heat-Related Illness Risk in Houston
text:
Results
Risk concentrated predictably around known vulnerability factors — older median age, higher poverty rates, and higher shares of residents living alone were all associated with elevated relative risk, on top of the baseline effect of temperature itself. Mapping the fitted relative risk by tract produced a clear visual: risk isn’t just “hotter tracts are worse,” it’s a compounding effect of heat exposure and social vulnerability.
The final deliverable was a public-health-style risk map and one-page prevention poster, translating the model into concrete guidance: stay hydrated, seek air-conditioned spaces, check on vulnerable neighbors, and never leave children in parked cars.

title: Mapping Heat-Related Illness Risk in Houston
text:
Why This Matters
This is a template that generalizes directly to other place-based public health and policy problems — disease surveillance, emergency resource allocation, or any question where “where” is as important as “how much.” It also demonstrates translating a technical spatial model into a plain-language product a health department could actually use.
Skills demonstrated: spatial statistics (CAR models), model diagnostics, working with messy shapefile/census data, translating technical results for a non-technical audience, R (spmodel, sf).

title: What Predicts an NHL Player’s Plus-Minus Score?
text: Hockey coaches want to recruit the best players, and players want to know which skills matter most — but “best” is hard to pin down with a single stat. Goals and points favor offensive players and undercount defensive contribution. We used plus-minus per game (a stat available to every skater, regardless of position) as a more balanced measure of overall effectiveness, and asked: which observable performance metrics actually predict it?

title: What Predicts an NHL Player’s Plus-Minus Score?
text: Hockey coaches want to recruit the best players, and players want to know which skills matter most — but “best” is hard to pin down with a single stat. Goals and points favor offensive players and undercount defensive contribution. We used plus-minus per game (a stat available to every skater, regardless of position) as a more balanced measure of overall effectiveness, and asked: which observable performance metrics actually predict it?

title: What Predicts an NHL Player’s Plus-Minus Score?
text:
Data & Method
We scraped NHL statistics covering the 2000–01 through 2024–25 seasons, aggregated by player, including position, assists, shots, shooting percentage, time on ice, and faceoff win rate. After exploratory analysis showed points-per-game was skewed and structurally biased toward offensive players, we settled on plus-minus per game as the response variable and fit a multiple linear regression:
\[\text{Plus-Minus/Game} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\text{Position} + \beta_2\text{Assists} + \beta_3\text{PIM/Game} + \beta_4\text{Shots/Game} + \beta_5\text{Shooting\%} + \beta_6\text{TOI/Game} + \beta_7\text{Faceoff Win\%} + \varepsilon\]
We validated the model with 1,000-iteration cross-validation rather than relying on in-sample fit alone.

title: What Predicts an NHL Player’s Plus-Minus Score?
text:
Results

Adjusted R² of 0.123 — the model explains a real but modest share of the variation, consistent with how much randomness exists in hockey outcomes
Cross-validated RMSE of 0.157, with an average prediction bias of 0.0001 (effectively unbiased) and low variability across 1,000 train/test splits, indicating the model is consistent even though its explanatory power is limited
Shooting percentage had the strongest positive association with plus-minus, followed by position (defensemen and centers), assists, and shots per game

title: What Predicts an NHL Player’s Plus-Minus Score?
text:
Honest Limitations
We were upfront that these effects, while statistically significant, are small in practical terms — the model captures general tendencies but isn’t precise enough to rank individual players confidently. Variables we didn’t have access to (age, coaching system, years of experience, team quality) likely explain more of the remaining variance than anything we could add from this dataset alone.

title: What Predicts an NHL Player’s Plus-Minus Score?
text:
Interactive Explorer
To make the underlying data browsable beyond the static report, I also built a Streamlit app letting users filter and explore NHL player statistics interactively: nhl-explorer.streamlit.app
Skills demonstrated: multiple linear regression, cross-validation for model assessment (bias/MSE/RMSE), web scraping, honest interpretation of modest effect sizes, deploying an interactive data app with Streamlit.
Final project for Regression Analysis (BYU Statistics, STAT 330), with Claire Peterson and Anzlei Larsen.

title: Data Acquisition Project
text:
This project analyzes publicly available CDC mortality data to uncover trends in causes of death across U.S. states and years. Using the CDC’s open API, I extracted and cleaned more than 10,000 records from the dataset bi63-dtpu. From there, I used Python’s pandas, matplotlib, and seaborn libraries to visualize national and state-level mortality patterns.
Plots were created using a combination of Seaborn and Matplotlib to balance style and customization. One of the key metrics explored is the AADR (Age-Adjusted Death Rate). This standardized rate accounts for differences in age distribution across populations: it sums the age-specific death rates for each age group and multiplies each by the proportion of a standard population in the same age group. This allows for fair comparisons between states and over time.
The data covers death and disease rates from 1999 to 2017, including both overall death counts and rates by specific causes. Mortality trends are a critical public health measure—they inform policy decisions, resource allocation, and highlight areas where healthcare disparities may exist.




Data Source
All data were pulled from the CDC’s public API endpoint:
CDC Mortality Data
This endpoint provides open, public domain data on deaths in the United States by cause, state, and year.
Data Collection and Cleaning
- Used Python’s requests library to query the API and retrieve JSON-formatted data.
- Converted the JSON into a Pandas DataFrame for analysis.
- Numeric fields (deaths, aadr, year) were converted from strings to numeric types for plotting and aggregation.
- Removed null or missing values, and filtered out the “All causes” category to focus on specific causes of death.
Analysis Goals
1. Identify the Top 10 causes of death nationwide.
2. Examine changes in total deaths by year.
3. Compare state-level Age-Adjusted Death Rates (AADR) to highlight regional differences.
Ethical Considerations
All data used in this project are publicly available through the CDC’s open data initiative. No private or identifiable information was accessed or used. The analysis follows good data practice by respecting API usage guidelines and ensuring proper citation of the source.





The top causes of death consistently include heart disease, cancer, and stroke. Heart disease remains the leading cause in most years, followed closely by various types of cancer.

National death counts show an overall increase from 2008 to 2017, with a slight decline between 2000 and 2008. These trends reflect demographic shifts and health crises over time, such as the opioid epidemic and aging population.

State-level AADR analysis reveals geographic disparities in mortality rates. Southern states such as Mississippi, Alabama, and Louisiana have higher average AADR values, indicating health inequalities that may be linked to socioeconomic factors, access to healthcare, or chronic disease prevalence.

Comparing trends by cause shows that some diseases, like diabetes and chronic lower respiratory disease, exhibit slow but steady increases, while others, like influenza and pneumonia, fluctuate more year-to-year.








This bar chart summarizes total deaths nationwide by cause. It highlights the persistent dominance of heart disease and cancer as leading causes. The chart allows for a quick comparison of relative mortality impact among causes.




This plot displays the average AADR by state. Southern states generally have higher rates, emphasizing regional health disparities. States with lower AADR, such as Hawaii and California, appear near the bottom, reflecting differences in public health interventions and population characteristics.




This line chart shows trends in national death counts from 2000 to 2017. It highlights periods of rising and falling mortality, providing context for policy changes and public health responses during those years.





Integrate additional CDC or NIH datasets to explore correlations between mortality and risk factors (e.g., obesity, smoking, socioeconomic status).

Perform regression analysis to model causes of death relative to demographic and regional predictors.

Develop an interactive dashboard using Streamlit or Dash to allow users to explore state-level trends dynamically.

Given the highest levels of obesity, heart failure and stroke, conduct further research into ways to both combat those causes of death and teach others to combat these diseases as well.

title: The Great Sleepover(option 1)
text:
Everyone has a camera (Option 2)

Your phone takes photos that once needed professional gear.


So why do people still pay photographers?



The camera was never the skill. Knowing what’s worth shooting, and whether the image is real, is.


Analytics is the same. Everyone has the camera now: dashboards, models, AI.

Soften the “15 years ago” claim from the old draft; “once needed professional gear” is safe and doesn’t invite a debate about camera specs. Everyone in the room loves analytics, so the point isn’t “you’re wrong,” it’s “the camera isn’t the skill.” Deliver it as an observation, not a challenge.

Youth sports costs have risen.
Travel and equipment can make participation difficult for families.


Use one or two verified figures from your original draft rather than trying to fit every statistic on the slide. Explain the source and year. The point is that sport can create belonging while access to sport remains unequal.

title: Sports managaement presentation
text:
A pipeline, not a guarantee
Girls’ participation in high school sports has grown dramatically over time.
That matters—but participation alone does not prove equal access, resources, or outcomes.

Use the Title IX and girls’ soccer numbers from the original deck after verifying them. Make the distinction between an encouraging trend and proof that every barrier has disappeared.

title: Sports managaement presentation
text:
Hope requires investment
What could it look like to make sport more accessible?

Fund the people and programs already doing the work.
Reduce the cost of getting started.
Follow local leadership.
Count who is still missing.


Keep the focus on practical steps rather than presenting an outside organization or individual as a savior.

title: Sports managaement presentation
text:
Who is still missing?
Sport can give strangers a shared identity.
But belonging is not automatic. We build it through the invitations we extend and the barriers we remove.

“I am because we are.”
Count who’s missing. Send the invitation.


Close by returning to the opening memory. Aim for about 30–40 seconds here. If the talk is running long, shorten the video first.

title: Sports managaement presentation
section: There are lies, damned lies, and statistics
text:
There are lies, damned lies, and statistics
A familiar line often attributed to Mark Twain.
But the important question isn’t whether statistics lie.
It’s whether we are asking them the right question.

Target: about 10 minutes. Be careful with the attribution: the saying is commonly attributed to Mark Twain, but the origin is disputed. You can say “a familiar saying” instead.

title: Sports managaement presentation
text:
A statistic can reveal—and hide

A statistic can show you something important while hiding the context that changes its meaning.

A model can calculate an answer correctly and still answer the wrong question.

This is a paraphrase, not a direct quotation. The point is not that statistics are useless, but that interpreting them requires context and judgment.

title: Sports managaement presentation
section: The model I thought I needed
text:
The model I thought I needed
In the BYU Sports Analytics Association, I worked on an NHL modeling competition.
The goal: predict the plus-minus leaders for hockey at the Winter Olympics.
My first instinct could have been to rely on historical Olympic data.
But there was a problem.

Briefly explain plus-minus for the audience: a player receives a plus or minus based on goals scored while they are on the ice at even strength, with some special-team situations excluded. Keep the exact definition consistent with the competition’s metric.

title: Sports managaement presentation
text:
The context changed
The 2026 Winter Olympics marked the return of NHL players to Olympic men’s hockey for the first time since 2014.
The 2025 Four Nations Face-Off offered recent best-on-best international hockey involving NHL players.
Past Olympic tournaments did not necessarily represent the same player pool or competition conditions.

Check the competition dates and your original analysis. The last Olympics with NHL players was 2014, not 2010. Be precise about which Four Nations statistics you used and why they were relevant to the prediction task.

title: Sports managaement presentation
text:
A better comparison
Instead of treating past Olympic results as automatically relevant, I used the Four Nations tournament as evidence for predicting the Olympic leaders.
The key decision was not just how to model the data. It was deciding which data were relevant.

Fill in the specifics before presenting: - Which Four Nations statistics did you use? - Did you combine them with regular-season NHL statistics? - How did you turn those data into a predicted ranking? - What was the competition’s scoring rule, and how did your entry perform?
Do not claim the change caused the win unless you can explain the scoring and comparison clearly.

title: Sports managaement presentation
section: Three questions before trusting a model
text:
Three questions before trusting a model
1. Relevance: Does the data resemble the situation I’m predicting?
2. Change: What is different this time?
3. Decision: Does the model answer the question the audience actually needs answered?

Return to the Olympics example for each question. The player pool and tournament context affected relevance; the Olympic format and timing affected what could reasonably be compared; the final goal was to predict leaders, not explain every aspect of hockey.

title: Sports managaement presentation
section: A model is not a substitute for judgment
text:
A model is not a substitute for judgment
Models help us organize evidence, quantify uncertainty, and make predictions.
But the analyst still has to decide:

What belongs in the data?
Which assumptions are reasonable?
What has changed since the historical examples?
What would make the prediction useful?


Avoid saying critical thinking is always better than modeling. In your story, critical thinking helped you select a more appropriate source of evidence. That is the stronger claim.

title: Sports managaement presentation
section: The point isn’t to reject statistics
text:
The point isn’t to reject statistics
It is to use them with care.
The number is not the whole story. The model is not the whole problem.

Ask the right question.
Choose relevant evidence.
Then decide how much to trust the answer.


End with the NHL story: the useful insight was noticing the context that made one source of evidence more relevant than another. Aim for a 30–40-second close.
